lessons.title: Attaching Event Listeners (addEventListener)
lessons.description: Learn how to make elements respond to user actions like clicks, key presses and form submissions.

sections.heading: What are events?
paragraphs: An event is anything that happens in the browser — a click, a key press, a form submission, a page load. JavaScript can listen for these events and run code in response. This is how pages become interactive.
list: Events are triggered by user actions or the browser itself
You attach a listener with element.addEventListener(event, handler)
The handler function runs every time the event occurs
You can attach multiple listeners to the same element

sections.heading: Removing listeners
list: removeEventListener(event, handler) — stops listening
You must pass the same function reference — not a new copy
Useful for temporary listeners (e.g., one-time modals)

codeExamples.heading: Basic click listener
explanation: addEventListener takes an event name and a callback function.
You can add multiple listeners — they all fire in order.
The callback runs every time the event occurs, not just once.

codeExamples.heading: Removing a listener with a named function
explanation: To remove a listener, you must pass the exact same function reference.
Named functions let you reference them for both add and remove.
Arrow functions create new references each time — you can't remove them easily.

practice.task: Add a click listener to a button that logs "Hello!" to the console. Then add a second listener to the same button that changes the button's text to "Clicked!".
hints: Both listeners will fire on each click.

keyTakeaways: addEventListener(event, handler) is the standard way to respond to events.
Multiple listeners can coexist on the same element.
To remove a listener, you must pass the exact same function reference.
Named functions are better than arrows when you need to remove listeners later.
lessons.challenge: Create a button that only works once — the first click shows an alert, then the listener removes itself so subsequent clicks do nothing.

lessons.title: Handling Mouse, Keyboard, and Form Input Events
lessons.description: The most common event types for user interaction — mouse, keyboard and form inputs.

sections.heading: Mouse events
list: click — button pressed and released
dblclick — double click
mousedown / mouseup — individual press/release
mouseover / mouseout — cursor enters/leaves an element
mousemove — cursor moves over an element (fires rapidly)

sections.heading: Keyboard events
list: keydown — key is pressed (fires repeatedly while held)
keyup — key is released
event.key — the key name ("Enter", "a", "ArrowUp")
event.code — physical key position ("KeyA", "Space")

sections.heading: Form events
list: submit — form is submitted (use preventDefault() to stop page reload)
input — value changes as user types
change — value changes and element loses focus

codeExamples.heading: Mouse and keyboard events
explanation: Mouse events let you respond to clicks, hovers and drags.
e.key gives you the key name — perfect for shortcuts.
Attach keyboard listeners to document since key events need a focused element or document-level listener.

codeExamples.heading: Form submission handling
explanation: preventDefault() stops the browser's default form submission (page reload).
e.target.value reads the current value of the input.
input event fires on every keystroke — ideal for live search.

practice.task: Create a form with a text input and a submit button. Prevent the default form submission and instead log the input value to the console.
hints: Read the value with input.value inside the handler.
Test that the page doesn't reload when you submit.

keyTakeaways: Keyboard events: keydown and keyup with e.key handle key presses.
Always use preventDefault() on form submit to stop page reload.
Use the input event for real-time value tracking as the user types.
lessons.challenge: Build a live character counter — an input field that shows the remaining characters (out of 140) as the user types, turning red when over the limit.

lessons.title: Working with the Event Object (event.target, event.key)
lessons.description: The event object carries useful information about what happened — target element, key pressed, mouse coordinates and more.

sections.heading: The event parameter
paragraphs: Every event handler receives an event object as its first argument. This object tells you exactly what happened, where it happened, and gives you control over it.
list: e.target — the element that triggered the event
e.currentTarget — the element the listener is attached to
e.type — the event name ("click", "keydown", etc.)
e.timeStamp — when the event occurred
e.preventDefault() — cancels the default behavior

sections.heading: Event-specific properties
list: Keyboard: e.key, e.code, e.ctrlKey
Mouse: e.clientX, e.clientY, e.button
Form input: e.target.value

codeExamples.heading: Using event.target and event properties
explanation: e.target is the actual element that received the event — crucial for delegation.
e.currentTarget is where the listener is attached — often the same as e.target.
Check e.key and modifier flags like e.ctrlKey for keyboard shortcuts.

practice.task: Add a click listener to a list element. Use event.target to detect which specific <li> was clicked and log its text content.
hints: Attach the listener to the parent <ul>.

keyTakeaways: e.target is the element that actually received the event.
e.currentTarget is the element the listener is attached to.
Event-specific properties like e.key and e.clientX tell you details about the event.
Use e.preventDefault() to cancel default behaviors like form submission.
lessons.challenge: Build a keyboard game where pressing arrow keys logs the direction (up/down/left/right) and pressing Escape shows "Game Over".

lessons.title: Preventing Default Browser Behaviors (event.preventDefault())
lessons.description: Stop the browser from doing what it normally would — form submissions, link navigation, context menus and more.

sections.heading: What is default behavior?
paragraphs: The browser has built-in actions for many elements — clicking a link navigates, submitting a form reloads the page, right-clicking shows a context menu. preventDefault() stops these from happening.
list: Form submit → page reload (prevent to handle with JavaScript)
Link click → navigation (prevent for SPA routing or analytics)
Right-click → context menu (prevent to build custom menus)
Spacebar on checkbox → toggle (prevent for custom behavior)
Drag and drop → browser drag behavior (prevent for custom drag)

codeExamples.heading: Preventing form submission and link navigation
explanation: preventDefault() on form submit is essential for JavaScript-driven forms.
Blocking link navigation is useful for single-page apps and analytics.
Preventing the context menu lets you build a custom right-click menu.
Only prevent defaults when you have a good reason — it changes expected behavior.

practice.task: Create a form that prevents page reload on submit, validates that the email field contains an "@" symbol, and shows an error message if it doesn't.
hints: Show errors by updating a <p> element's textContent.

keyTakeaways: preventDefault() stops the browser's built-in action for an event.
Most commonly used on form submit to prevent page reload.
Also useful for blocking link navigation and context menus.
Only prevent defaults when you're replacing the behavior with your own JavaScript.
lessons.challenge: Build a link-based navigation menu where clicking links doesn't navigate away — instead it updates the page content dynamically using JavaScript.
